verdict.headline: Treasury tripled its bond buyback and long-term rates rose anyway as oil topped $100
verdict.label: The ten-year reached 4.857%, its highest since November 2023, and the thirty-year added about five basis points to 5.30% on the day Treasury sized its first expanded buyback at up to $6 billion; WTI settled near $96.70 and the S&P 500 fell 0.48% to 7,636.36 for a third straight decline, with the Russell 2000 off 1.32% and Meta up 6.55%
verdict.rationale_short:
The Treasury put its largest liquidity-support bid yet under long-dated debt on Wednesday and the long end rose regardless. The first operation of the expanded program was sized at up to $6 billion, triple the $2 billion originally communicated to investors, with future operations at least $4 billion through November 4. The ten-year yield still reached 4.857%, its highest since November 2023, the thirty-year added about five basis points to 5.30%, and the two-year rose three basis points to 4.42%, its highest since July 2024.

That is the day's information, and it is about demand rather than flow. A buyer of that size failing to hold the market flat does not mean the marginal seller was crowded out; it means the seller was met. Through Wednesday morning the entire repricing of this week sat in the two-year, which is a Fed-response signal. The close added the ten- and thirty-year, which is not: it prices inflation the Fed does not fully offset, plus term premium for the fiscal path underneath.

Crude supplied the input. WTI settled near $96.70, up close to 4% and the highest since May, with Brent above $101 — clearing the $95 threshold that had held all week by more than a dollar and a half. Both levels this morning's report named as the pair that would mark the shift, WTI through $95 and the ten-year through 4.818%, broke in the same session. That report was right about which levels mattered and wrong to leave the quiet long end as possibly mechanical pending several buyback operations; the first operation resolved it in one session, and in the direction it treated as the less likely.

Equities fell a third straight day. The S&P 500 lost 0.48% to 7,636.36, the Nasdaq 0.64% to 26,253.34 and the Dow 405.41 points to 52,380.66, while the Russell 2000 dropped 1.32% to about 2,921 — nearly three times the large-cap decline, because small caps carry more floating-rate and near-dated debt, so a move at the long end reaches interest expense directly rather than through a multiple. The clearest evidence sits in what did not help: Meta closed up 6.55% at $653.69 on the launch of its Muse agent, and a 6.5% gain in a top-weight mega-cap still left the index lower. That locates the selling in the discount rate, not in earnings. Energy was one of only two sectors higher, at 0.63%.

The evidence is not one-directional. Long-dated yields rose as much as five basis points before easing, so the session's high is not the same as a settled repricing, and a single operation is a thin basis for judging a program that runs to November 4. Europe took the move harder than the US — the FTSE fell 1.38%, the DAX 1.6% and the CAC roughly 2% — which is consistent with an energy-cost shock as much as with a US rates story, and the dollar was little changed at 98.83 rather than bid, which an inflation-scare repricing would more usually produce.

What would change the picture: the ten-year holding above 4.818% through Thursday's PPI would confirm the break as a repricing rather than an event spike, and a close back underneath while the operations continue would say the long end was overwhelmed by one day's news rather than changing its mind. On the thirty-year, a close above 5.33%, August 18's nineteen-year high, would say the expanded program is being absorbed at the maturity it targets most directly. Two August inflation prints land first — PPI Thursday with headline expected near 5.3% and core 4.6%, CPI Friday at a consensus 0.3% month over month and 2.9% year over year — and neither can contain this week's crude, so a hot print would say pass-through was already running before the barrel got here. Futures price roughly 57% odds of a quarter-point hike on September 16.
verdict.lede_short: Treasury sized its first expanded buyback at up to $6 billion, triple the original plan, and the long end sold off into it anyway: the ten-year reached 4.857%, its highest since November 2023, and the thirty-year added five basis points to 5.30%. Both levels this morning's report named — WTI through $95, the ten-year through 4.818% — broke in the same session. Meta rose 6.55% and the S&P 500 still fell 0.48%, which puts the selling in the discount rate rather than in earnings.

supporting_data.label: Treasury's first operation under the expanded program will buy up to $6 billion of longer-dated debt, triple the $2 billion originally communicated, with future operations at least $4 billion through November 4 — the largest mechanical bid Treasury has placed under the long end, and yields rose into it rather than falling

The ten-year Treasury yield reached 4.857%, its highest since November 2023, and the two-year rose three basis points to 4.42%, its highest since July 2024 — 4.818% had held for five sessions and gave way on the day the offsetting bid was tripled
The thirty-year yield rose about five basis points to 5.30% — the level it traded through twice in August without closing above, and the maturity the buyback targets most directly
WTI settled near $96.70, up close to 4% and the highest since May, with Brent above $101 — $95 was the threshold that had held all week, and crude cleared it by more than a dollar and a half

Meta closed up 6.55% at $653.69 after launching Muse, an autonomous agent sold in $20 and $100 monthly tiers — a top-weight mega-cap added 6.5% and the S&P 500 still fell 0.48%, which locates the day's selling in the discount rate rather than in earnings

Canada's retaliatory tariffs of 15% to 50% on nearly $20 billion of US goods took effect September 8, and the administration moved to strike Canadian-origin products from federal schedules worth more than $50 billion a year — a second cost-push input arriving in the same week as $100 crude and two inflation prints

watchlist_mentions.note: Closed up 6.55% at $653.69 after launching Muse, an autonomous agent that books travel, completes web forms and manages payments, sold in $20 and $100 monthly tiers alongside a free one. It is the company's first tiered AI subscription. The move is notable less for its size than for what it failed to do: a 6.5% gain in a top-weight name left the S&P 500 down 0.48%, which is the session's cleanest evidence that the selling was in the discount rate.

Fell about 2% as Meta's agent launch was read as a direct claim on general-purpose search and assistant demand. An eight-and-a-half-point spread between two mega-caps on one product announcement is a rotation within the sector rather than a verdict on it.

Closed down 0.28% after announcing the iPhone Duo, its first foldable, at roughly $2,000, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro line and a $100 increase on older models still sold new. A near-flat close on the largest hardware change in the product's history says the launch was in the price; the pricing-power question it raises is not resolved by the event itself.

WTI settled near $96.70, up close to 4% and the highest since May, clearing the $95 threshold that had held all week; Brent traded above $101. The level tracked here now moves to $100 on WTI. Thursday's EIA weekly petroleum report at noon carries the first supply figures since the Saudi outages.

Slipped about 0.3% to near $78,250, holding $78,000 for an eighth session below $80,000. It did not take a bid from the long-end selloff and did not break with equities either, which continues to leave it detached from both the haven trade and the rates trade.

trade_setups.thesis: The level held for five sessions and gave way on the session Treasury tripled its buyback operation to as much as $6 billion, with the yield reaching 4.857%, its highest since November 2023. A mechanical bid of that size failing to hold the market flat is evidence the marginal seller was met rather than crowded out. Against that, long-dated yields rose as much as five basis points before easing, so the session high is not yet a settled repricing.
trade_setups.entry: 4.818% is the level that broke; 5.00% is the next round threshold above it. Thursday's PPI is the first real inflation input to test it.
trade_setups.invalidation: A close back under 4.818% while the buyback operations continue would say the long end was overwhelmed by one day's news rather than changing its mind about inflation.
trade_setups.horizon: Thursday and Friday, into the September 16 FOMC

trade_setups.asset: The thirty-year at 5.30% against the buyback program
trade_setups.thesis: The thirty-year added about five basis points to 5.30%, the level it traded through twice in August without closing above, and it is the maturity the expanded program targets most directly. The program runs from September 9 to November 4 with operations of at least $4 billion after the first, so the number of operations run is the variable that separates absorbed supply from purchased calm. One operation is a thin basis for judging either.
trade_setups.entry: 5.30% is where it sits; 5.33%, August 18's nineteen-year high, is the level above it. The count of completed operations is the second variable.
trade_setups.invalidation: The thirty-year falling back through 5.19%, where it traded after the August 19 expansion was announced, would say the program is working at the maturity it targets and the week's move was the front end's story.
trade_setups.horizon: Through November 4, tested first on Thursday

trade_setups.asset: Two August inflation prints that predate $100 crude
trade_setups.thesis: PPI lands Thursday with headline expected near 5.3% and core 4.6%; August CPI follows Friday at a consensus 0.3% month over month and 2.9% year over year, core 0.3% and 3.1%. Both cover August and cannot contain this week's move above $100. Futures price roughly 57% odds of a quarter-point hike on September 16, which would take the target range to 3.75%-4.00%, and the FOMC is in blackout through September 17 so no official can frame either print.
trade_setups.entry: 0.3% month over month on core CPI is the consensus line; the September print that can carry $100 Brent is not released until October, after the decision.
trade_setups.invalidation: Prints at or below consensus would say pass-through had not reached the consumer even at August's energy levels, which would make this week's curve move look early rather than prescient.
trade_setups.horizon: Thursday and Friday, into the September 16 decision
